messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 39
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Construction Worker
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 73

He is a 39-year-old North American man who works in construction and has spent most of his adult life on job sites where the work is physical, noisy, and measured in concrete poured, beams raised, and deadlines met. Before the event that changed him, he describes himself as steady and easygoing, the kind of person who could handle long days, bad weather, and hard labor without carrying much home with him. He was married then, and his life felt anchored by routine: early mornings, packed lunches, the drive to whichever site needed him, and evenings that belonged to his wife and their small routines together.

That changed when he witnessed a violent accident at work. He had been on a multi-level build, moving materials with a crew he knew well, when another worker fell from a height and struck the ground below. The moment comes back to him with vivid force: the sound first, then the stillness, then the sudden rush of voices and panic. He remembers freezing for a second before forcing himself to move. He is not the one who falls, but he is the one who sees it happen, and that image becomes lodged in him with an intensity he did not expect. In the days after, he keeps replaying the scene, especially the instant before the fall, as if some detail hidden there might explain how it happened or how it could have been prevented.

At first he tries to push through. Construction has never rewarded hesitation, and he is used to keeping his head down and getting back to work. But he starts sleeping poorly, waking in the middle of the night with his heart racing and his mind already back on the site. He feels keyed up in a way he cannot turn off, scanning corners, heights, and moving equipment with an almost painful vigilance. Loud bangs, the scrape of metal, or someone shouting across a job site can jolt him into a sudden rush of fear before he realizes where he is. He is embarrassed by how quickly his body reacts, and that embarrassment makes him more withdrawn. He stops talking about the incident with coworkers and tells himself that if he can just stay busy enough, it will settle down.

Instead, his world narrows. He begins avoiding parts of the job that remind him of the accident, especially scaffolding and upper levels. He volunteers for tasks on the ground when he can, telling others that he prefers the work closer to home base, but inside he is arranging his day around what he can tolerate. Even then, he feels on edge. He checks equipment repeatedly and has trouble trusting structures that used to feel ordinary. He notices himself scanning exits in restaurants and sitting with his back against a wall in waiting rooms. When he drives, he becomes tense around overpasses and construction barriers. His body seems to anticipate danger before his mind can catch up.

He also grows more distant at home. His marriage, already under strain before the accident, does not survive the months that follow. He is harder to reach emotionally, more irritable, and often absorbed by thoughts he does not want to share. His wife tells him he is present only in pieces. He hears her, but he does not know how to explain that he feels split between the life in front of him and the one that keeps intruding from behind. He becomes ashamed of how often he thinks about the man who fell and of how helpless he felt in that moment. There are times when he pictures the scene so clearly that he has to leave the room or step outside to breathe. At other times, he feels strangely numb, as if he is watching his own life from a distance.

Over time, he begins to measure his days by what he is able to endure. He shows up for work, but it takes more effort than it once did, and by the end of the day he is exhausted in a way that sleep does not fix. He remains vigilant, uneasy, and easily startled. He is not the man he was before the accident, and he knows it. He speaks of the event with a kind of grim loyalty, as though telling the story plainly is the only way to keep it from taking over completely, even though it already shapes how he moves through nearly everything now.
